title: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH HYPOTONIA, POOR GROWTH, DYSMORPHIC FACIES, AND AGAMMAGLOBULINEMIA

relationships.phenotype: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH HYPOTONIA, POOR GROWTH, DYSMORPHIC FACIES, AND AGAMMAGLOBULINEMIA

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, poor growth, dysmorphic facies, and agammaglobulinemia (NEDHGFA) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SEL1L gene.

paragraphs.text: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, poor growth, dysmorphic facies, and agammaglobulinemia (NEDHGFA) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by infantile-onset developmental delay, intellectual disability, severe axial hypotonia, microcephaly, short stature, failure to thrive with repeated vomiting after eating, and facial dysmorphism, combined with infantile-onset agammaglobulinemia with absent mature B cells. Affected individuals suffer recurrent severe respiratory and other infections requiring immunoglobulin replacement therapy and die at early ages (Weis et al., 2024).

Weis et al. (2024) designated the disorder in their patients ENDI-agammaglobulinemia (ENDI-A) syndrome, distinguishing it from the ERAD-associated neurodevelopmental disorders with onset in infancy (ENDI) syndromes reported in an accompanying paper, in which agammaglobulinemia was not a feature.

Weis et al. (2024) reported 5 developmentally delayed children with agammaglobulinemia, all born into a large family of the Roma population living in an isolated region of southern Slovakia; the patients were the offspring of 2 pairs of consanguineous parents within that family. Patients 1 and 2 (IV-1 and IV-2) were born in 2006 and 2014 to one consanguineous couple, and patients 3 to 5 (IV-3, IV-5, and IV-6) were born in 2009, 2014, and 2016 to another consanguineous couple. The clinical presentation was uniform among the 5 patients. All had problems with food intake soon after birth with repeated vomiting after eating, were unable to gain weight, had pale skin, gradually developed cachexia, and had similar facial dysmorphisms including triangular faces and big ears. All showed severe axial hypotonia and general developmental delay with short stature and microcephaly, and all had intellectual disability and were unable to speak words or sentences. Three patients (patients 1, 3, and 5) could not sit up, hold their heads, or raise their heads while supporting themselves on their elbows; only patient 4 was able to sit without support, at the age of 4.5 years.

The patients described by Weis et al. (2024) were frequently admitted to hospital because of recurrent severe lower respiratory infection almost every month, beginning with otitis media and sinusitis (bilateral maxillary and ethmoidal) and progressing to bronchitis and pneumonia; during pneumonia the children developed respiratory insufficiency often caused by food aspiration. In patients 3 and 4, hearing impairment was diagnosed at 1 year of age, which the authors considered likely secondary to multiple otitis media. Immunologic testing of peripheral blood from patients 3, 4, and 5 revealed no detectable mature CD19+ memory B cells in the circulation and no circulating immunoglobulins at the age of 12 months and beyond. Although the absolute numbers of CD4+ helper and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells were largely in the normal ranges, the ratio of CD4+ to CD8+ T cells was reduced, which the authors interpreted as pointing to impaired T-cell development. A gut biopsy of patient 3 showed subtotal villous atrophy of the duodenum as Marsh IIIb enteropathy with no CD20+ B cells and moderate to high amounts of CD3+, CD4+, and CD8+ intraepithelial cells compared with noncarriers. Patient 4 had COVID-19 infection with respiratory failure at the age of 7.7 years; after administration of therapeutic anti-SARS-CoV-2 monoclonal antibodies the viral load decreased effectively, but the course of treatment was prolonged and differed from that of healthy children or children with X-linked agammaglobulinemia, and no COVID antigen-specific memory T cells were detected in peripheral blood.

In the individual case descriptions given by Weis et al. (2024), patient 1 (IV-1) had hypotonia, developmental delay, frequent vomiting after eating, facial dysmorphism, and agammaglobulinemia since birth; at 15 months she had a 30% weight deficit representing dystrophy of the third degree (marasmus), and at 3 years of life she had short stature (-3.28 SD), underweight (-5.81 SD), microcephaly (-1.89 SD), and severe developmental delay. She was treated for acute renal failure and pulmonary hypertension and died of multiorgan failure at the age of 2.9 years. Patient 2 (IV-2) had axial hypotonia and facial dysmorphism since birth, developed bronchopneumonia, and died suddenly 2 months after birth; her immunoglobulin levels were not tested. Patient 3 (IV-3) was born at 37 weeks' gestation with a birth weight of 2,700 g and length of 48 cm and normocephaly, and had a ventricular septal defect; brain MRI performed because of an episode of unspecified epilepsy showed normal myelinization, and he was treated with valproate. Genetic testing for cystic fibrosis and for the hereditary agammaglobulinemia-BTK gene was negative. At 2.5 years he had short stature (-2.62 SD) and was underweight (-4.21 SD); he was exhausted from severe sepsis and died from respiratory failure. Patient 4 (IV-5) had brain MRI at 10 months showing unspecific leukoencephalopathy frontally and occipitally bilaterally without seizures; at 6 years she could turn, sit with support, and tried to stand with support but did not speak; at 4.5 years she had short stature (-3.12 SD), underweight (-3.03 SD), and microcephaly (head circumference 43 cm, -2.83 SD). Eye examination showed palpebral ptosis with bilateral partial papillary atrophy, and laboratory testing showed sideropenic anemia, increased folate, and hypovitaminosis D. Patient 5 (IV-6) was born at 39 weeks' gestation (3,025 g, 50 cm) with microcephaly (head circumference 31 cm); at 2.5 years he had short stature (-2.25 SD), was underweight (-2.64 SD), and had microcephaly (-2.64 SD), hypotonia, and severe developmental delay. Brain MRI showed leukoencephalopathy frontally, parietally, and occipitally bilaterally, and at 4.5 years discrete supratentorial cortical atrophy; he had no seizures. Eye examination showed bilateral palpebral ptosis and bilateral papillary excavation, and he had micropenis, central hypothyroidism, hypoplastic thymus, hepatopathy, and dystrophic nails. He died at 5.1 years of severe pneumonia and respiratory failure. The authors noted that all 3 of patients 3, 4, and 5 had a sudden dramatic deterioration of the clinical condition due to sepsis with multiorgan failure.

Weis et al. (2024) noted that individual IV-4 in the family, a girl who carried 1 allele of the SEL1L C141Y variant, was born with severe hypotonia, alobar holoprosencephaly, and multiple malformations, including cheilognathopalatoschisis, 1 nostril with a missing part of the nasal wings, "frog" eyes with an almost closed vision field, low-set deformed ears, microcephaly, short neck, pterygium colli, narrower chest, a transverse groove on the left hand, 4 fingers in claw-like position on the right hand, malformed toes with polydactyly and syndactyly of the fourth and fifth toes, a malformed anus, multiple joint contractures, and congenital heart defects with atrial ventricular septum defect and patent ductus arteriosus. She died at 9 days of age from cardiorespiratory failure. The authors stated that this patient had no infection or problem with immunity as in the other sibs with agammaglobulinemia.

The transmission pattern of NEDHGFA in the family reported by Weis et al. (2024) was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. The 5 affected children were born to 2 pairs of consanguineous parents within a single large family; the biallelic SEL1L C141Y variant was confirmed in all 5 affected individuals but not in the parents or in unaffected sibs, and the pedigree was interpreted by the authors as showing autosomal recessive inheritance.

In 5 patients from a large consanguineous Slovakian (Roma) family with NEDHGFA, ascertained through the web-based tool GeneMatcher, Weis et al. (2024) identified homozygosity for a c.422G-A transition (c.422G>A, NM_005065.6) in exon 4 of the SEL1L gene, resulting in a cys141-to-tyr (C141Y) substitution. Array comparative genomic hybridization in patients 4 and 5 did not reveal any larger deletions or amplifications within the genome, and whole-exome sequencing of patients 3 and 5 and their parents (III-3 and III-4) did not identify any known monogenic inborn errors of neurologic disorders and agammaglobulinemia; because both patients were born to the same consanguineous parents, variants were filtered under the assumption of recessive inheritance with 100% penetrance and by allele frequency (less than 1% or unknown) and predicted deleteriousness. Two variants were identified in individual patients, SEL1L p.Cys141Tyr and FAR2 p.Arg490Trp (c.1468C-T, NM_001271783.2); the FAR2 variant was excluded as causal because Sanger sequencing confirmed its segregation with symptoms in patient 2 only and because loss of FAR2 function is not linked to neurologic disorder or agammaglobulinemia. Sanger sequencing confirmed the biallelic SEL1L C141Y variant in all 5 patients, but not in parents or unaffected sibs. The variant was considered pathogenic with a total score of 14 points based on ACMG criteria. The authors also sought a second biallelic variant that might account for the immune phenotype: other variants associated with neurodevelopmental disorders or hypogammaglobulinemia were examined with chromosome analysis, SNP array, and next-generation sequencing, which did not show any other genomic imbalances or associated genetic variants. They nonetheless acknowledged that disease causality could not be firmly established without a knockin mouse model carrying the variant.

Weis et al. (2024) compared the SEL1L C141Y variant with the hypomorphic SEL1L M528R and G585D and HRD1 P398L variants described in an accompanying paper by generating knockin HEK293T cells expressing the individual variants. C141Y cells had the lowest SEL1L and HRD1 protein levels and the highest protein levels of the ERAD substrates CD147 and IRE1-alpha, indicating the most severe ERAD dysfunction among the variants. Clinically, whereas the other ENDI patients were in their teens and 20s, the 5 patients with the C141Y variant exhibited B-cell depletion and agammaglobulinemia and died at very early ages as a result of frequent infections. The authors concluded that functionality of SEL1L-HRD1 ERAD is inversely correlated with disease severity in humans.

Weis et al. (2024) showed that the mutation affects a conserved residue in the luminal N-terminal fibronectin type II (FNII) domain of SEL1L, a domain of unknown function that is not conserved in invertebrates. Position-specific scoring matrix analysis indicated that cysteine at this position was evolutionarily selected and that the cys-to-tyr substitution might be detrimental to SEL1L function. Structural modeling of the human SEL1L-HRD1-OS9-DERLIN1 complex with AlphaFold2 showed 2 short antiparallel beta sheets connected by 2 long random coils at the FNII domain, with 2 disulfide bridges in close, quasiorthogonal juxtaposition: Cys141-Cys168 and Cys127-Cys153.

In skin fibroblasts derived from patients compared with those from noncarrier individuals, Weis et al. (2024) found that SEL1L protein levels were significantly reduced and largely undetectable, and that HRD1 protein levels were also significantly reduced, by over 90%; the reduction was confirmed by immunofluorescent staining of patient fibroblasts and immunohistochemical staining of duodenal biopsies from patients. The reduction was not due to altered gene transcription, as mRNA levels were unchanged. SEL1L and HRD1 proteins became unstable in patient cells treated with cycloheximide, while the known ERAD substrates IRE1-alpha and CD147 accumulated and were stabilized. Unexpectedly, the lectins OS9 and ERLEC1 were also significantly decreased and destabilized in patient cells, uncoupled from their gene transcription. A model ERAD substrate, the proarginine vasopressin mutant G57S, formed significantly more high-molecular-weight aggregates in SEL1L C141Y knockin HEK293T cells than in wildtype cells, to levels similar to those in ERAD-knockout cells, and ER volume was increased in the knockin cells. ER chaperones BiP and protein disulfide isomerase were significantly elevated in patient fibroblasts, but IRE1-alpha was not phosphorylated and XBP1 mRNA splicing was not detected, and there was no difference in the percentage of phosphorylated PERK and eIF2-alpha after normalization to total protein, leading the authors to conclude that the variant causes severe ERAD dysfunction without an overt unfolded protein response.

Weis et al. (2024) found that, on overexpression, SEL1L C141Y had no effect on the interactions between SEL1L and the other ERAD components OS9, ERLEC1, HRD1, and UBE2J1, excluding interference with complex formation. Disruption of the other disulfide bond by generation of SEL1L C127Y knockin HEK293T cells similarly reduced the protein levels of the ERAD complex and stabilized known ERAD substrates, although the effects of both variants were milder than those in SEL1L-null HEK293T cells, suggesting that C141Y is not a complete loss-of-function variant, which the authors suggested may explain why the patients could survive for months or even years. Deletion of the entire exon 4 encoding residues 115 to 170 (FNII-less SEL1L) caused only an approximately 60% reduction of SEL1L protein with a C-terminus-specific antibody and a 30% reduction of HRD1, with mild if any changes in ERAD substrate levels, indicating that the FNII domain itself is dispensable for SEL1L-HRD1 ERAD function and that the C141Y variant acts through the unpaired cysteine. Treatment with the proteasomal inhibitor MG132 elevated the protein levels of both SEL1L and HRD1, and deletion of HRD1, but not of RNF5, significantly rescued the protein levels and stability of SEL1L in C127Y and C141Y knockin cells, with accumulated SEL1L C141Y forming high-molecular-weight aggregates. The authors concluded that the variant causes proteasome-mediated self-destruction of the SEL1L-HRD1 ERAD complex.

Weis et al. (2024) proposed that the SEL1L C141Y variant causes agammaglobulinemia by blocking B-cell development in humans, noting that SEL1L-HRD1 ERAD plays a key role in B-cell development in mice as a checkpoint controlling the degradation and abundance of the pre-B-cell receptor, and that SEL1L-HRD1 deficiency in the B-cell lineage causes developmental blockade at the large pre-B-cell stage with significant reduction of mature B cells. They stated that definitive evidence would come from further studies with mouse models carrying the variant.

Weis et al. (2024) reported that their patients were hospitalized nearly monthly and treated with antibiotics and sufficient oxygen supply and were regularly supplemented with immunoglobulins. IgG was given as replacement therapy every 4 weeks in patients 3, 4, and 5, after which a substantial improvement in acute infections was noted, although chronic respiratory symptoms, phlegm, and cough continued to recur in some forms. The authors considered that the early treatment strategy of IgG replacement therapy and antiinfectious prophylaxis very likely postponed infectious complications in these 3 patients, although all 3 were observed to have a sudden dramatic deterioration of the clinical condition due to sepsis with multiorgan failure.

The 5 patients reported by Weis et al. (2024) were raised from birth in a big family of the Roma population living in an isolated region in the southern part of Slovakia, and were the offspring of 2 consanguineous couples within that family.

Ji et al. (2016) studied the role of the Sel1L-Hrd1 ERAD complex in B-cell development in mice. B-cell-specific Sel1L-deficient mice generated by crossing Sel1L flox/flox mice with CD19-Cre mice were born in a normal mendelian ratio and appeared healthy with no obvious growth defects, but spleen weights were significantly reduced, the percentage of peripheral B cells in spleen, blood, and lymph nodes was reduced by 60 to 75%, and absolute numbers of splenic B cells were more than 75% lower than in controls, while CD4+, CD8+ T, and myeloid cells were not affected. Within the pro-/pre-B-cell compartment of the bone marrow, surrogate light chain-positive CD2-negative pre-B I and large pre-B (II) cells were twice as numerous, whereas small pre-B cells were reduced by 50%, indicating a severe developmental defect at the transition from large to small pre-B cells; the defect was not accounted for by cell death and was independent of Chop.

Mechanistically, Ji et al. (2016) showed that protein levels of 3 main components of the pre-B-cell receptor (pre-BCR) complex were dramatically increased in the pro-/pre-B cells of Sel1L-deficient mice, with a 3-fold increase in the percentage of lambda-5+ Igmu+ large pre-B cells, while transcript levels of VpreB, lambda-5, and Igmu were comparable, indicating posttranscriptional regulation. In Sel1L-knockdown or Hrd1-null 70z/3 pre-B cells, steady-state levels of all 3 pre-BCR components increased and the half-life of Igmu protein increased from approximately 60 min to over 120 min, proteasome inhibition increased Igmu stability, and ubiquitination of Igmu was dramatically reduced. Sel1L deficiency increased ER exit and surface levels of the pre-BCR, with increased phosphorylation of Syk and a more than 50% increase in cycling pro-/pre-B cells in bone marrow. The pre-BCR, but not the mature BCR, was an ERAD substrate, and pre-BCR degradation required BiP but was independent of the unique region of lambda-5.

clinical_synopsis.feature: Duodenal subtotal villous atrophy (Marsh IIIb enteropathy)
Repeated vomiting after eating since birth
Failure to gain weight, cachexia, marasmus
Hearing impairment diagnosed at 1 year of age in 2 patients
Death in early childhood (2 months to 5.1 years)
Absent speech; unable to speak words or sentences
Global developmental delay with onset in infancy
Respiratory insufficiency, often with food aspiration

allelic_variants.name: SEL1L, CYS141TYR

paragraphs.text: In 5 patients from 2 consanguineous couples within a large Roma family from southern Slovakia with neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, poor growth, dysmorphic facies, and agammaglobulinemia (NEDHGFA), Weis et al. (2024) identified homozygosity for a c.422G-A transition in exon 4 of the SEL1L gene (NM_005065.6), resulting in a cys141-to-tyr (C141Y) substitution at a conserved residue in the luminal N-terminal fibronectin type II domain. The variant was found by whole-exome sequencing of patients 3 and 5 and their parents under a recessive model, and Sanger sequencing confirmed the biallelic variant in all 5 patients but not in parents or unaffected sibs. The variant disrupts the Cys141-Cys168 disulfide bond; patient skin fibroblasts showed SEL1L protein that was significantly reduced and largely undetectable and HRD1 protein reduced by over 90%, with accumulation and stabilization of the ERAD substrates IRE1-alpha and CD147, and knockin HEK293T cells carrying the variant showed the most severe ERAD dysfunction among 4 disease variants tested. Deletion of HRD1 rescued SEL1L protein levels, indicating proteasome-mediated self-destruction of the complex. The variant was classified as pathogenic with a total score of 14 points based on ACMG criteria. An individual in the family carrying 1 allele of the variant (IV-4) was born with alobar holoprosencephaly and multiple malformations and died at 9 days of age without immune abnormality.

agent.process_note: I read both papers in the folder in full. Weis et al. (2024) is the only paper reporting patients; from it I took the family structure (5 affected children of 2 consanguineous couples in one large Roma family in southern Slovakia), the individual case descriptions in the Human subjects section (birth years, growth SD scores, MRI findings, ages and causes of death), the immunologic findings in patients 3, 4, and 5, the SEL1L c.422G>A (p.Cys141Tyr) variant and its NM_005065.6 annotation, the exclusion of the FAR2 p.Arg490Trp variant, and the functional work in patient fibroblasts and knockin HEK293T cells. Ji et al. (2016) contains no patient data and is used only for the mouse/cell-line B-cell developmental work on Sel1L-Hrd1 ERAD and the pre-BCR, cited under Animal Model. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so I did not state a gene MIM number or chromosomal location, and I could not find either in the papers. The accompanying paper by Wang et al. describing the other ENDI variants is not in the folder, so those variants are mentioned only as cited within Weis et al. (2024) for comparison. Numbers in Table 1 and Table 2 of Weis et al. were not available in the text file (titles only), so no tabulated immunoglobulin or lymphocyte values are quoted.
